title: Changelog immutability + retention notes (enterprise security/compliance)
content:
Purpose
- Capture proposed approach for (1) immutable/tamper-evident storage of customer-visible model changelog entries and (2) retention/records management expectations.
- Provide copy/paste answers for common enterprise security questionnaires (fintech/healthcare customers keep asking “how do you ensure release notes can’t be altered retroactively?”).

Context (why this exists)
- Today: model updates are communicated inconsistently (docs pages + Slack messages + occasional runtime release notes). Enterprise customers are treating “model change logs” as change-management artifacts.
- Desired: customer-visible release notes generated from a canonical model registry + signed change events (see ADR-0127). Need a defensible story on immutability + retention.

Working definitions (align terminology)
- Model metadata: internal registry record (includes internal-only fields + customer-safe allowlist).
- Change event: append-only event emitted when a model version is created/updated/deprecated, including actor + timestamp + diff summary.
- Changelog entry: customer-visible record derived from one or more change events after review/approval; can be “superseded” but not edited in-place.
- Audit log events: security/audit stream for create/update/deprecate + publish actions (separate from customer changelog feed, but correlated via IDs).

Threat model (what we’re trying to prevent)
1) Silent retroactive edits to published customer-visible release notes.
2) Inability to prove “who changed what, when” for model metadata and publication actions.
3) Accidental deletion or truncation of history.
4) Leakage of internal-only model details into customer-visible feeds.

Non-goals (v1)
- Proving “content is correct” (only that it is traceable + non-tampered post-publication).
- Customer-specific per-tenant changelog narratives.
- Cryptographic transparency log with third-party witnessing (can be Phase 2).

Proposed architecture (v1) – immutability + tamper-evidence
Source of truth
- Model registry database remains source of truth for metadata records.
- Change events are emitted on create/update/deprecate operations and stored in an append-only event store.
- Changelog generator consumes events, renders a draft entry, routes through approval workflow, then publishes an immutable “published entry” record.

Immutability guarantees
A) Append-only event storage
- Every change event is written as a new record (no update-in-place) with a unique event_id.
- Event record includes:
  - actor (user/service principal)
  - actor_type (human/service)
  - timestamp (RFC3339)
  - registry_entity (model_id, version_id)
  - change_type (create/update/deprecate)
  - diff summary (customer-safe subset + internal full diff stored separately)
  - previous_event_id (for per-entity chaining)

B) Hash chaining (tamper-evidence)
- Each change event stores a hash of its canonical serialized payload plus the hash of the previous event in that entity’s chain.
- This provides tamper-evident sequencing: modifying a past event breaks subsequent hashes.
- Note: this is “tamper-evidence,” not absolute prevention. Prevention is handled via access controls and storage controls; evidence via hash chain.

C) Signed publication artifacts (customer-visible)
- When a changelog entry transitions to PUBLISHED, the generator/publisher:
  - produces a canonical JSON representation of the customer-visible entry
  - computes a digest (SHA-256)
  - signs the digest using a dedicated signing key (KMS-managed) OR a service-level signature mechanism (implementation pending platform team decision)
  - stores signature + key_id + signing_time with the published entry
- Docs-site publish job and API feed serve the same canonical JSON; the signature allows internal verification that the published entry has not been altered.

D) No “edit published entry” operation; use supersede
- If a published entry is wrong/confusing, we do not edit it. We publish a new entry that supersedes the previous one.
- Superseding entry references:
  - supersedes_entry_id
  - reason (customer-safe)
  - link to internal incident / support ticket
- The UI should render “Superseded on YYYY-MM-DD” and show the corrected entry.
- This pattern is explicitly required for audit defensibility and matches our internal expectations for regulated customers.

E) Storage controls (immutability in practice)
- Customer-visible published entry artifacts stored in an immutable-friendly store:
  - Primary: database table with “append-only / no updates” enforced at application layer + DB permissions
  - Secondary (recommended): object storage write-once pattern (bucket with versioning + retention lock, if supported in our cloud), storing the canonical JSON blob by entry_id
- Even if we start with DB-only, we should structure so we can add object-store “ledger copies” without changing contracts.

F) Redaction / allowlist control to prevent leakage
- Generator only uses public_changelog_fields allowlist.
- Any field not in allowlist must not be serialized into the customer-visible canonical JSON.
- Docs CI linting should fail templates that reference internal-only fields.

G) Audit log emission (who/what/when)
- In addition to the changelog entry itself, we generate audit events for:
  - model metadata create/update/deprecate
  - changelog entry draft created
  - approval requested
  - approved/rejected
  - published
  - superseded
- Audit log is exportable to SIEM with immutable retention policy (see retention section).

RBAC + separation of duties (what we should be able to claim)
- Separate permissions for:
  - editing model metadata (Registry Editor)
  - approving customer-visible release notes (Release Notes Approver)
  - publishing (Release Notes Publisher)
- For enterprise posture, it’s preferable if “approver” and “publisher” can be separate roles (even if same person can be in both roles initially).
- All privileged actions require SSO + MFA (per Redwood baseline), with actions attributable to a human identity unless explicitly performed by a service principal.

Retention policy (proposal for v1)
This section is written to support questionnaires; details can be refined with GRC/legal.

1) Customer-visible published changelog entries
- Retention: retain indefinitely (or “for the lifetime of the service”) as part of product documentation and customer change-management record.
- Rationale: customers expect historical model change logs; deletion creates trust issues and complicates incident retrospectives.
- Deletion: only allowed under exceptional circumstances (legal requirement). If deletion is required, retain internal audit record that deletion occurred, including legal basis.

2) Draft entries + review comments
- Retention: 18 months (proposal) for drafts/comments.
- Rationale: enough for operational debugging and support follow-ups; doesn’t need to be permanent.
- Note: approvals and publish actions are separately retained in audit logs per below.

3) Change events (append-only)
- Retention: 7 years (proposal) to align with common enterprise expectations for audit trails.
- Rationale: supports reconstructing what changed even if customer-visible notes are minimal.

4) Security audit logs (create/update/deprecate/publish)
- Retention: 7 years (proposal) with immutable storage controls.
- Export: SIEM export supported; customers often ask for “audit logs available on request” vs “self-serve.” For now: internal export process; later: customer-facing audit API may be an add-on.

5) Backups
- Backups follow platform backup standards; retention and immutability per infra policy (not duplicated here). Make sure we can answer “are backups immutable?” carefully (usually: encrypted, access-controlled, limited admin access; not always WORM).

6) Customer feed endpoints (RSS/JSON)
- The feed is a view over published entries; retention is implied by published entries retention.
- Practical note: we may cap pagination window for performance (e.g., last N entries per request), but that is not “retention.” Make this clear in customer comms.

What we can truthfully claim (draft language)
- “Published model release notes are append-only. Corrections are handled by publishing a superseding entry, and the original published entry remains available for audit/history.”
- “All model metadata changes and publication actions are logged with actor identity and timestamps, and audit logs are retained for at least 7 years.” (Confirm final duration with GRC.)
- “We use role-based access control and approval workflows to limit who can publish customer-visible release notes.”
- “We apply a strict allowlist for customer-visible fields to prevent internal-only information from being published.”
- “We maintain tamper-evident chaining/signing of changelog artifacts to detect retroactive modification.” (Don’t oversell as ‘tamper-proof.’)

Common enterprise questionnaire Q&A (copy/paste)

Q: Are your model release notes immutable?
A: Published model release notes are treated as append-only records. We do not edit published entries in place. If a correction is needed, we publish a new entry that supersedes the prior entry while preserving the original. Publication actions are audit logged with actor identity and timestamps.

Q: How do you prevent retroactive tampering?
A: Access to publish is controlled via RBAC and an approval workflow. In addition, published changelog artifacts are stored as canonical records and are signed/hashed (tamper-evident). Any retroactive modification would be detectable via signature/hash validation and audit logs.

Q: Do you log “who changed what and when”?
A: Yes. Model metadata changes (create/update/deprecate) and changelog publication actions are recorded as audit events including actor identity, timestamps, and the affected model_id/version_id. Audit logs can be exported for security review as needed.

Q: What is your retention period for changelog and audit logs?
A: Published customer-visible changelog entries are retained for the lifetime of the service. Audit logs and model change-event history are retained for at least 7 years (subject to our records policy). Draft working artifacts are retained for a shorter period.

Q: Can Redwood delete or modify existing release notes?
A: In normal operation, Redwood does not modify existing published entries; changes are made through superseding entries. Deletion would be exceptional and handled through a controlled process with audit logging.

Q: Do customers get an RSS/JSON feed of updates?
A: Yes (planned/rolling out). Customers can subscribe to a machine-readable feed of published model changelog entries. Each entry includes the model/version identifiers, publication date, and a link to the full release note.

Q: Do you support evidence for change-management (e.g., SOX, SOC2, regulated processes)?
A: We provide an auditable record of model metadata changes and customer-visible release note publication, including timestamps and actor attribution, plus retention aligned to enterprise expectations.

Q: How do you ensure internal or sensitive details don’t leak into customer notes?
A: Customer-visible release notes are generated from a strict allowlist of fields and validated against a schema. Template linting and automated checks prevent internal-only fields from being published.

Implementation notes / gotchas (internal)
- Be careful with “immutability” claims. Security reviewers will ask whether admins can alter DB rows. Our posture should be:
  - “append-only at application + permission layers”
  - “tamper-evident via cryptographic chaining/signing”
  - “audit logs and restricted admin access”
  - optional: “object storage retention lock” if we implement WORM.
- Make sure rollback/correction UX uses “supersede” semantics; do not call it “edit.”
- Ensure deterministic canonicalization for hashing/signing (field ordering, normalization, timestamps). If we sign, we must sign the canonical JSON bytes.

Open questions (need decisions)
1) Do we implement KMS signing in v1, or start with hash chaining only?
2) Do we need an object-storage WORM copy for published entries to satisfy certain procurement teams (FinchBank-type accounts), or is append-only DB + signatures sufficient?
3) Final retention durations (7 years vs 3 years) need GRC sign-off.
4) How do we handle pre-migration history gaps in a compliant way (i.e., “historical notes may be incomplete prior to YYYY-MM-DD”)? Coordinate with Support messaging.

Next steps / owners
- Kevin Osei: align retention language with records policy + review with Olga (GRC).
- Marcus Lin + Jordan Lee: validate RBAC language and ensure publish role checks match implementation.
- Naomi Feldman: review customer-facing claims (“tamper-evident” wording) and approve questionnaire responses.
- Connor O’Brien: confirm operational process for corrections (supersede flow) during release freezes.

Last updated notes
- 2026-02-22: Added explicit “tamper-evident vs tamper-proof” language and clarified draft retention vs published retention.
